stl_001: Missouri state champion American elm. Measurements: MDC 2010 marker and 2014 release: 191 in circumference, 102 ft tall, 122 ft spread, 324 pts (measured 2 July 2010). The current MDC champion layer lists 208 in, 102 ft, 127 ft, 342 pts (girth_cm 528 taken from this; 2017 MDC release says a Kansas City-area elm 'toppled the old record held by a St. Louis elm scoring 342', so it lost the title in May 2017 but this is the same tree; it is now a FORMER champion). Age: St. Louis Magazine (Beer Barons piece) says estimated about 200 years; the Arbor Day piece (2019, updated Feb 2025) says thought to be older than the cemetery (founded 1849). Both are vague; age left broad. Survived Dutch elm disease. Recognisable: stands in front of the McDonnell and Maritz burial plots (aerospace magnate James S. McDonnell chose his plot partly for the tree), Block 308 on Walnut; more than 100 ft tall with a 122 ft crown, far larger than the other trees there. A state champion marker 'American Elm, Missouri State Champion Tree, Great St. Louis Tree Hunt #9' (erected 2010 by MDC, Missouri Botanical Garden and Gamma Tree Experts) stands at it. PIN: coordinate is the HMdb marker position 38.68742,-90.22607 (a user-submitted marker location); the MDC champion layer puts it ~500 m away at 38.68797,-90.23183 (cemetery-level, fuzzed). Two coordinates disagree, so approximate, cemetery-level. ALIVE: flagged. lifecheck.py gave NONE (no iNaturalist record); the latest source describing it as standing is stlmag Arbor Day article updated Feb 2025 and the HMdb page revised May 2026 (page does not state condition). Bellefontaine also lost its champion shingle oak in 2022 (removed after decline), so check the elm is still there before promoting. Photo candidates: none seen; HMdb marker photos exist but not licence-checked.
stl_002: Missouri State Champion and (since 2009 per the Garden) National Champion white basswood. CONFLICT in figures: MDC Conservationist 2016 and the MDC champion layer give 158 in circumference (401 cm), 87 ft (26.5 m) tall, 84 ft crown, 266 pts (used here); the Garden's own tree page quotes 'the state' as 103 ft and 12.4 ft / 149 in circumference. Both from the same state programme at different dates; unclear which is newer. Recognisable: by the Museum Building near Tower Grove House; the Garden says a former state champion possumhaw stands 'right across the path'. The Garden installed lightning protection with a copper ground, removed turf beneath it to reduce root competition and avoids soil compaction (MDC 2016). Pin is the MDC champion layer coordinate (38.61202,-90.25777), about 50 m from Tower Grove House at ~38.6115,-90.2584; approximate. ALIVE: lifecheck RECENT 2026-09-06 (iNaturalist observation within 150 m, not necessarily this tree) plus MDC 2016 feature. Ticketed ground: 1 of the 2 MBG trees kept in this city.
stl_003: ONE SOURCE (the owner of the ground, Missouri Botanical Garden; the second MBG fact page repeats it, not independent). The Garden's tree page: after a coring project that counted rings in representative trees, 'the oldest tree in the Garden is a bald cypress just south of Shoenberg Fountain near the Administration Building, thought to be planted around 1874'; probably part of Henry Shaw's arboretum, which he began in 1861. Another Garden page (via search snippet only, not read) instead names three bald cypresses along Alfred Avenue near the maintenance gate as the oldest, probably offspring of the originals; the Garden's own wording says no one knows the oldest for sure because of missing records. Age therefore stated as 'thought to be planted around 1874' (=~150 yrs, age_min 140 age_max 160, source-derived). Bald cypress drop their needles in winter, which the Garden says saved them from St. Louis coal smoke that killed nearly all its evergreen conifers. Pin: Shoenberg Fountain is at 38.61060,-90.25827 (Nominatim); the tree is 'just south', so the pin is the fountain minus a few metres: approximate. No girth or height published. ALIVE: lifecheck RECENT 2025-07-13 near the fountain (iNaturalist, not tree-specific). Interpretive signs on Garden trees give each tree's story. Second ticketed MBG tree (2 of 7 in this pass).
stl_004: Park-owned source (Tower Grove Park's GPS interactive map, Tree Walk): 'this large circle of osage-orange trees was strategically planted' in the late 19th century 'as a turnaround for a horse-drawn carriage'; it also says 'near the Music Stand ... another strategically planted grouping of osage-orange, arguably the oldest trees in the park'. St. Louis Post-Dispatch 'hidden gems': an Osage orange among the trees by the music stand is 'likely the oldest tree in the park', more than 150 years old. St. Louis Magazine (Arbor Day, updated Feb 2025) quoting the park arborist: grouping near the Music Stand along South East Drive, 'likely planted in the late 1800s or early 1900s'. These two dates conflict (150+ vs late 1800s to early 1900s) so age stays broad, 120 to 170. NOTE: the pin here is the park map's pin for the Osage-orange CIRCLE (38.60488,-90.24482); the Music Stand grouping and the circle may be two different places. The stlmag text places the grouping 'near the pond and the Piper Palm House' (Palm House is ~1.1 km west at 38.6078,-90.2572), which does not match the map pin, so the Music Stand grouping location is unconfirmed; do not claim it is the same as the circle. Tree Walk cluster: stl_004, stl_005, stl_006 are all on the park's Tree Walk within ~250 m of each other (east side, near the Sons of Rest Shelter). Recognisable: a ring of Osage-oranges (knobby, orange-peel bark; softball-sized green fruit in autumn) forming a circle that once turned carriages. ALIVE: lifecheck RECENT 2026-08-29 (iNaturalist within 150 m, not tree-specific); the park map page is current. Tower Grove Park is a Level II accredited arboretum with ~6,800 trees (2016 inventory), designed with Henry Shaw.
stl_005: ONE SOURCE (the park, owner of the ground; map pin 38.60417,-90.24714 on the park's GPS Tree Walk). Park's description: 'king of the hill and sitting at the highest point of the park, this oak is wider than it is tall', with 'gigantic, over-extended branches'; the name comes from the bark resembling American chestnut. No girth, height or age published. Species given as 'Chestnut Oak' (Quercus montana, formerly prinus); Latin name not on the park page, added from the common name, flag. Pin is the park's map pin, a published point for this stop but not verified on one crown: approximate. Recognisable: widest-spreading oak on the park's highest ground, with deeply furrowed dark bark. About 70 m from the Osage circle (stl_004) and 90 m from stl_006. ALIVE: lifecheck RECENT 2026-09-02 (iNaturalist, not tree-specific).
stl_006: ONE SOURCE (the park; Tree Walk map pin 38.60497,-90.24594). Park text: 'the largest of the three rock elms in Tower Grove Park and ... a spectacular specimen. Measuring just over 100 feet tall' (about 30.5 m; height from the park, not a measurement of ours). Tight skyward form; susceptible to Dutch elm disease like American elm; the park injects it every three years to prevent the disease, which otherwise 'would ensure certain death'. A rock elm champion exists elsewhere (Ulmus thomasii, 196 in, 79 ft, private land in St. Louis County) so this is not a state champion. No girth or age published. Recognisable: tallest elm on the Tree Walk, columnar. 'Rock elm' is not common in cities. ALIVE: lifecheck RECENT 2026-08-26 (iNaturalist, not tree-specific); the DED injection programme is current park practice. Pin approximate (park's pin, not verified on one crown).
ind_002: Pin is an estimate at the Temple Ave / Brookside Pkwy S Dr intersection from OSM street geometry (Temple Ave runs at about lon -86.1181, Brookside Pkwy S Dr crosses at about lat 39.7858); no source publishes a coordinate at the trunk. View-only: private lot, but the huge canopy overhangs Brookside Parkway and the sidewalk was built with a cutout around the trunk (Weekly View 2014), so the tree is clearly seen from public ground (Hidde 2026-11-04 rule); pin on the viewing corner. MEASUREMENT: Springdale Neighborhood Association says in late 2023 it measured 88 ft high, 20 ft 3 in circumference (=617 cm), average crown spread 126.5 ft; monumentaltrees.com (facts only) lists girth 6.17 m measured Jan 2024, consistent. Height 88 ft = 26.8 m. AGE: neighbourhood site 'estimated at 400 years'; WFYI 2014 'almost 400 years, almost 18 ft around' (older measurement); Weekly View 2014 'experts say 300 to 400 years'; monumentaltrees lists 401 +/- 20 (2025 entry) and an older 276 +/- 50 (2018); Conflict in age is wide (270 to 450), all estimates, no ring count. Age basis source (vague, repeated vaguely). Claimed by locals as the largest chinkapin oak in Marion County and possibly oldest tree in the city (the Kile Oak, ind_001, also claims oldest: two of our pages must not claim the same crown, writer should say 'among the oldest'). History: 2007 'most huggable and remarkable tree' contest win and mayoral proclamation (per earlier lead notes, WFYI); when the city planned to straighten the sidewalks and fell it the owners negotiated a cutout; drivers have scarred the bark over the years; 2014 oak lace mite infestation and deadwood, neighbourhood raised donations for treatment (WFYI, AP); the tree is the symbol of Springdale Neighborhood Association (HUNI lists it as landmark). ALIVE: late 2023 measurement plus Jan 2024 monumentaltrees measurement; lifecheck.py gave only unrelated iNat plant observations (not tree evidence). RECOGNISE: the only huge broad-crowned oak on this corner, canopy overhanging Brookside Parkway, sidewalk bends round the trunk, bark scarred on the street side. Walk pair with ind_003 (Nowland Oak, about 350 m west). Indiana DNR Heritage Trees page also names it (per earlier pass lead; not re-fetched, www.in.gov/dnr/forestry/8169.htm hung this pass). Commons photo: none checked.
ind_003: Small pocket park, narrow lot about 45 m long (OSM leisure=park way 1383750446, bbox lat 39.78574-39.78617, lon -86.12192 to -86.12178; Nominatim); pin is the park centre, so approximate with location_site. The oak is the park's reason to exist: a neighbour (Chris Hartley, then president of Springdale Neighborhood Association) spotted it in 2012 behind a house slated for demolition; once the house came down the size showed; the neighbourhood won a 2016 GreenSpace grant to protect the lot; park celebrated 20 May 2017 with tile markers in the sidewalk linking it to the Temple Oak and Spades Park; plants, art and interpretive panels (Indiana Historical Society) planned around the 'tree circles'. AGE CONFLICT: Weekly View 2017 'over 300 years' (began growing about 1716); KIB 2018 '296 years after it was planted' in 2012 (so about 1716); KIB 2016 'approximately 200 years old'. Source basis, vague; no measurement published (no girth or height found). ALIVE: thin; latest source dated 2018 (KIB) and the park appears on OSM; no 2023+ report seen; flagged, writer should not claim current condition beyond 'saved in 2012, park since 2017'. Tell apart: the only large oak in the pocket park on the north side of Nowland Ave, the tree circle and plantings round it. Walk pair with ind_002 (Temple Oak), about 350 m east along Brookside Parkway South Drive; the neighbourhood's own tour route also runs through Spades Park. No Commons photo checked.
ind_004: Grown from a seed flown round the Moon on Apollo 14 (February 1971) by astronaut Stuart Roosa; planted 9 April 1976 at a ceremony led by Governor Otis R. Bowen (NASA NSSDCA). NASA gives position approx 39 deg 46.099' N, 86 deg 9.721' W = 39.76832, -86.16202: east side of the Statehouse, N. Capitol Ave side, about 100 ft south of the Oliver P. Morton statue and about 50 ft back from the street. NASA's own figure is 'approx' and the lawn arboretum holds 21 species and 44 trees planted in 2017 (Indiana Public Media), so approximate; the tree is unmarked, so the writer should say how to find it (Morton statue, then 100 ft south). Plaque at coordinates approx 39.76747, -86.16270 (south side). Islands.com (Dec 2024) says it 'towers over the Statehouse', about 50 years old, one of the surviving Moon Trees in Indiana (Islands says three; Atlas Obscura summaries say four, so do not state a count). ALIVE: Islands.com 21 Dec 2024 describes it standing; NASA page undated about status. No girth or height found anywhere. Young by the project's age standards (49 years); qualifies on historic significance, not age. Conflict: none on species. Atlas Obscura also has a page 'indianapolis-moon-tree' (finding aid, not used).
lxk_001: Kentucky state champion American basswood (Fayette/Lexington cemetery). KY champion listing (fetched 2026-11-04) gives circumference 292 in (742 cm), height 78 ft (23.8 m), crown 73 ft. Search summaries (not fetched, so unrecorded as fact) also carry American Forests figures 276 in / 102 ft, listed national champion in 2017 and later displaced by a Pennsylvania tree; do not claim 'national champion' or 'largest in the world' as fact: the cemetery's own claim is 'largest in the world' and Waymarking records a plaque at the base calling it the largest in the United States, with Wikipedia noting the National Register puts the largest in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. Waymarking (user posted 2007): plaque dated 1987 says the tree was alive at the signing of the US Constitution (1787), i.e. about 230 years then; that plaque age is a claim, not a measurement, and 2007 plaque 230 yrs now 250+ if taken at face value. Plaque also states height 60 to 80 ft, spread 40 to 60 ft, which conflicts with the register. Heights disagree across sources (78 / 101 / 102 ft); record both. Pin: Waymarking GPS 38.057633,-84.507617 (N 38 03.458, W 084 30.457), 'just behind the monument to Henry Clay's grave'; confirmed on the basis of a published GPS fix at the tree plus a plaque at its base. A plaque (National Arborist Association, per a 2011 geocache description) stands near it. Alive: Waymarking log 2025-09-20; iNaturalist observation within range 2026-06-28 (lifecheck RECENT). Where to stand: behind the Henry Clay monument, look for the plaque. Photo candidates: none checked (Commons search found nothing).
lxk_002: The park's own site says the bur oak has stood an estimated 300 years and that all visitors should try to see it. The marker beside it (Society of Colonial Wars in the Commonwealth of Kentucky with Lexington Parks and Recreation, text read at hmdb.org via web.archive.org copy) says 'estimated to be more than 250 years old' and that the tree stood witness from William McConnell's claim in the 1700s, the Westbrook Stock Farm of the late 1800s, to the park's formation in the 1990s. Ages conflict (250+ vs 300); record broad 250 to 300, source-based, no measurement. No girth or height found. Pin is the marker's coordinate (HMDB: 38 03.207 N, 84 31.802 W), which stands at the tree; kept approximate because the marker, not the trunk, is the fix. Recognition: a huge hollow-trunked bur oak with its limbs long enough to reach across the trail and propped on tall supporting poles ('crutches') per a 2022 poem on lexpomo.com quoting the park forester (trunk mostly hollow, too few rings to count, so age uncertain); the only marked old oak in the park. Geocaching text says a second old bur oak fell in the February 2003 ice storm, this is the survivor. Alive: iNaturalist observation 2025-10-13 within lifecheck range (RECENT); 2022 poem and March 2022 marker photos show it standing. Commons candidates, not judged: File:Bur oak.JPG (2015-03-23, McConnell Springs), File:Bur oak, North American white oak.JPG, File:North American white oak, bur oak.JPG. Lexington's official city tree is the bur oak. Free city park; nothing behind a ticket.
hsv_001: ONE SOURCE + PIN ONLY AT PRESERVE LEVEL (findable gate not met: no photo, no confirmed pin, no named small site; writer must decide, probably lead-grade). City trail page (owner of the ground) says this is the largest known shellbark hickory in Alabama: 179 inches around (4.75 ft diameter), 96 ft tall, average crown spread 74 ft. Girth 455 cm = 179 in x 2.54; height 29 m = 96 ft. CONFLICT: Wikipedia's Alabama Champion Tree Program table (an older snapshot) lists the Madison County shellbark hickory (added 2007) at 102 in, 112 ft, 90 ft spread, so the city's figures probably are a later remeasure or a different tree; do not quote the Wikipedia numbers. Where: the city's sign list puts it after the Beaver Dam; a visitor post (Steve Jones, 3 Nov 2022) puts the champion water tupelo within a few hundred yards of the champion hickory, near the tupelo slough (old Flint River oxbow) reached from the Flint River picnic area; a photo point on the trail is near the hickory. The pin recorded is the Wikipedia coordinate for the whole 538-acre preserve (34.64556, -86.46722), NOT the tree. No GPS for the trunk found. Recognise: a very large hickory on drier upland ground just off the slough, with the champion tupelo a short walk away. Alive: 2022 visitor account places both champions on the trail; city page current. Candidate for a Commons photo: none found (Category:Hays_Nature_Preserve has 2 files, titles unseen).
hsv_002: ONE OFFICIAL SOURCE PLUS ONE DATED EYEWITNESS; PIN AT PRESERVE LEVEL ONLY (same coordinate as hsv_001, the Wikipedia coordinate for the whole preserve, not the tree). The city trail page lists 'State Champion Water Tupelo' trees (plural, no figures; sign appears after the Cave in Limestone section) and notes the trunks shelter wood ducks, screech owls and fox squirrels; flowers feed tupelo honey. Steve Jones (a retired forester's blog, visit 3 Nov 2022) reports a State Champion water tupelo with a ground-line diameter of 'a good nine feet' (his estimate, buttressed base), the moss skirt on the trunk marking the usual winter water line at about navel height, standing in the oldest oxbow slough, within a few hundred yards of the champion hickory (hsv_001); Hampton Cove golf course is visible across the slough and a limestone ledge 8-10 ft above flood level is nearby. Wikipedia's Alabama champion table (older snapshot) lists a Madison County water tupelo (added 2007) at 237 in circumference, 112 ft, 88 ft spread; not confirmed on a fetched official page, so no girth recorded. Recognise: the large buttressed tupelo with a moss line on its trunk in the slough. Age: none; do not derive. Two champion tupelos may be meant by 'trees', so the writer should keep it to 'a champion'. Same findability caveat as hsv_001.
bha_001: Alabama's state champion green hawthorn, named by the Alabama Forestry Commission in Nov 2025 (Bham Now, 20 Nov 2025: 'this week'). Nominated by Jefferson County Greenways volunteer Larry Stephens, who researched its history and received a commemorative plaque. Origin per Greenways: sprouted along a fence row in Ware, a mining community, around 1900; unknown whether planted or bird-sown; called 'a living monument to a past time'. Bham Now: planted late 1800s, about 125 years old. Age conflict is mild (late 1800s vs around 1900): kept broad, 100 to 130, source-stated not derived. Neither fetched page gives girth, height or crown. Search snippet of Forestry Commission 2025 PDF row (NOT a fetched page, a lead only, do not publish figures): '52 30 44 93' possibly circumference 52 in, height 30 ft, spread 44 ft, 93 points; PDF unreadable here (forestry.alabama.gov refuses connection; wayback copy truncated at 5 MB, no pdftotext). So girth_cm/height_m left empty. Location: the park coordinate is Wikipedia's park centre (33.4454, -86.8622), NOT the tree; only descriptive position known: BMRR South Trail across from the Pollinator Garden, which Greenways places at the far west end of the South BMRR Trail #3. Approximate until a GPS fix or the champion-tree plaque position. What makes it recognisable: a hawthorn (a small, thorny, multi-branched tree, not an oak or pine) opposite the pollinator garden, and a champion-tree plaque presumably marks it (Stephens received a commemorative plaque; whether on-site not confirmed). Alive: 2025 designation, 2025 news (WVTM13 unveiling 19 Nov 2025, page returned 451 to fetch, not used as source). One-source flag: two fetched pages are both Greenways/Bham Now from the same event, partly dependent; US one-credible-source rule applies (Alabama Forestry Commission designation). Lifecheck not run (no tree coordinate). A reader pin or GPS fix would turn this confirmed.
